title: 8. Async / Concurrency / Queues
description: Turing FDE + Andela core: JS event loop, microtask queue, promises, async/await edge cases, worker threads, Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS, backpressure, concurrency patterns.

8.1 JS Event Loop & Microtasks: Call stack → Web APIs → Callback queue → Event loop
Microtasks (Promise.then, queueMicrotask) drain BEFORE next task
setImmediate (Node) runs after I/O callbacks, before timers on next iteration
process.nextTick runs before any other microtask
Avoid blocking the event loop: offload CPU work to worker threads
8.2 Promises & async/await: Unhandled rejection = process crash in Node 15+
Promise.all fails fast; Promise.allSettled never rejects
Promise.any returns first fulfilled; AggregateError if all reject
async function always returns a Promise — return value is wrapped
8.3 Worker Threads / Child Processes: worker_threads: shared memory via SharedArrayBuffer + Atomics
child_process.fork: separate V8 instance, IPC channel
cluster: fork workers that share a TCP server port
Use workers for CPU-bound (image resize, crypto, JSON parse >5MB)
Workerless alternative: offload to job queue + separate process
8.4 Kafka: Offset committed per consumer group per partition
At-least-once default; exactly-once via transactions API
Retention by time (7d default) or size
Consumer lag = latest offset − committed offset; alert on sustained lag
8.5 RabbitMQ / SQS: SQS: visibility timeout hides message from other consumers during processing
SQS FIFO: exactly-once, 300 TPS limit (3k with batching)
Dead-letter queue: after maxReceiveCount (SQS) or x-max-retries (RabbitMQ)
SQS long poll (WaitTimeSeconds=20) vs short poll
8.6 Backpressure: Backpressure = signal from consumer to producer to slow down
Node streams: write() returns false → pause source until drain event
Kafka consumer: pause partition, process, resume
Queue depth + consumer lag as primary alert signals
Token bucket / leaky bucket as rate-limiting at ingestion layer

options.text: A D B C
A D C B
A B C D
A C D B

questions.explanation: Synchronous first (A, D), then microtasks drain (C — Promise.then), then macrotask queue (B — setTimeout). Microtasks always run before the next macrotask.

questions.prompt: In Node.js, which runs FIRST after the current synchronous code completes?

options.text: setTimeout callback
Promise.then callback
process.nextTick callback
setImmediate callback

questions.explanation: process.nextTick runs before all other I/O callbacks and before Promise microtasks. Order: nextTick queue → microtask queue (Promise.then) → I/O → setImmediate → setTimeout(0).

questions.prompt: What happens if a Promise.then callback always schedules another Promise.then?

options.text: It works fine — each .then is a separate macrotask
The microtask queue never empties — I/O callbacks and timers are starved
Node.js automatically pauses after 1000 microtasks
The call stack overflows

questions.explanation: Microtasks drain completely before the event loop moves to the next macrotask phase. An infinite chain of Promise.then calls starves all I/O, timers, and setImmediate — the equivalent of blocking the event loop.

questions.prompt: Inside a Node.js I/O callback, which fires first: setImmediate or setTimeout(fn, 0)?

options.text: setTimeout(fn, 0) — timer phase comes first
setImmediate — check phase comes before timers when inside an I/O callback
Depends on the OS scheduler
They fire in the same phase

questions.explanation: Inside an I/O callback the event loop is already past the timers phase. The next phase is check (setImmediate), so setImmediate always wins inside I/O callbacks. Outside I/O context the order is non-deterministic.

questions.prompt: Which of these BLOCKS the Node.js event loop? (select all)

options.text: JSON.parse of a 50MB string
fs.readFile (async)
crypto.pbkdf2Sync
A for loop iterating 10M items
await fetch(url)

questions.explanation: Anything synchronous and CPU-heavy blocks the single JS thread. fs.readFile is async (I/O handled by libuv thread pool). await fetch suspends the coroutine but does not block the event loop. JSON.parse, pbkdf2Sync, and tight loops are all synchronous.

questions.prompt: You call 5 APIs in parallel. One may fail but you want results from all that succeeded. Which is correct?

options.text: Promise.all — it collects all results
Promise.allSettled — returns all results regardless of rejection
Promise.race — picks the fastest
Promise.any — ignores rejections

questions.explanation: Promise.allSettled never rejects. Each element has {status: 'fulfilled'|'rejected', value|reason}. Promise.all short-circuits on first rejection. Promise.any resolves on first success (not all). Promise.race is irrelevant here.

questions.prompt: In Node.js 15+, what happens to an unhandled promise rejection?

options.text: It is silently swallowed
A warning is printed but the process continues
The process crashes with a non-zero exit code
The rejection is re-thrown on the next tick

questions.explanation: Since Node 15 the default unhandledRejection mode is 'throw', which crashes the process. Node 12-14 emitted a DeprecationWarning. Always attach .catch() or try/catch in async functions.

options.text: Promise { 42 }
Promise { <pending> }
undefined

questions.explanation: async functions always return a Promise. The value 42 is the resolved value, but at the moment console.log runs synchronously the Promise is still pending (it resolves in the microtask queue). You'd see Promise { <pending> } in most runtimes.

questions.prompt: Promise.any([p1, p2, p3]) — all three reject. What happens?

options.text: Resolves with undefined
Rejects with the first rejection reason
Rejects with an AggregateError containing all reasons
Stays pending

questions.explanation: Promise.any rejects with an AggregateError (errors property = array of all reasons) only when ALL input promises reject. This is the only case where it rejects.

options.text: Nothing — sequential awaits are fine
Requests are sequential instead of parallel — O(n) latency instead of O(1)
The loop exits before all promises resolve
await inside for-of is a syntax error

questions.explanation: Sequential awaits serialize all requests. For independent fetches, use Promise.all(ids.map(fetchUser)) to run them in parallel and collect results in O(1) wall-clock time.

options.text: Yes — the try/catch wraps the entire async function
No — the rejection happens asynchronously after try/catch exits
Yes — Promise rejections always surface to the nearest catch
Depends on whether doWork uses throw or Promise.reject

questions.explanation: Without await, the promise returned by doWork() is floating. The try/catch only catches synchronous throws. The rejection propagates as an unhandled rejection, not caught here. Always await, or attach .catch().

questions.prompt: When should you use Node.js worker_threads over child_process.fork?

options.text: Worker threads are always faster — use them for everything
worker_threads for CPU-bound tasks needing shared memory; fork for isolated processes (shell commands, separate apps)
child_process.fork for CPU tasks; worker_threads for I/O
They are identical — just different APIs

questions.explanation: worker_threads share memory via SharedArrayBuffer + Atomics, low IPC overhead, same process memory space. fork creates a separate V8 instance with its own heap — better isolation but higher startup and IPC cost.

questions.prompt: You want to fully utilize 8 CPU cores for an HTTP server. What's the right tool?

options.text: worker_threads — share the HTTP port across threads
cluster — forks N worker processes that share the same TCP port
async/await — JS is already multi-threaded
setImmediate loop to spread work

questions.explanation: cluster.fork() creates child processes that each run the full server and the master uses round-robin (or OS) load balancing across the shared port. For HTTP servers, cluster is the standard pattern; worker_threads are for background CPU tasks, not serving.

questions.prompt: Which tasks are worth offloading to a worker thread? (select all)

options.text: Parsing a 100MB JSON file
Fetching data from a remote API
Generating a PDF (puppeteer / pdfmake)
bcrypt hashing with cost factor 14
Reading a 2KB config file

questions.explanation: CPU-bound tasks (JSON parse of large payloads, PDF generation, bcrypt with high cost) block the event loop and should go to a worker thread or job queue. Network I/O (fetch) is non-blocking by nature. Small file reads are fast and use libuv's thread pool already.

questions.prompt: Why do you partition Kafka messages by tenant_id?

options.text: To encrypt messages per tenant
Messages with the same key always go to the same partition, guaranteeing ordering per tenant
To limit partition count
Kafka requires string keys

questions.explanation: Kafka guarantees ordering only within a partition. Keying by tenant_id means all events for a tenant land in the same partition → same consumer → ordered processing per tenant without coordination.

questions.prompt: What is 'consumer lag' in Kafka and why do you alert on it?

options.text: Time since last broker heartbeat
Number of unprocessed messages = latest offset − committed offset; sustained lag = consumers falling behind producers
Replication delay between brokers
Network latency to the broker

questions.explanation: Consumer lag = latest offset in partition − consumer group's committed offset. Rising lag means producers are outpacing consumers → eventual queue overflow or processing delay. The primary SLO signal for Kafka consumers.

questions.prompt: Your Kafka consumer processes a payment and then commits the offset. The process crashes after processing but before committing. What happens on restart?

options.text: The message is lost — offset was never committed
The message is reprocessed — at-least-once delivery
Kafka detects the crash and skips the message
The transaction is rolled back automatically

questions.explanation: Default Kafka semantics are at-least-once. On restart the consumer reads from the last committed offset and reprocesses the message. For payments, make the downstream operation idempotent (dedup by message_id) or use Kafka transactions for exactly-once.

questions.prompt: What replication factor and min.insync.replicas combination gives strong durability for a production Kafka cluster?

options.text: RF=1, min.insync=1
RF=3, min.insync=2 with acks=all
RF=2, min.insync=1
RF=5, min.insync=5

questions.explanation: RF=3 tolerates 1 broker failure. min.insync.replicas=2 with producer acks=all means at least 2 replicas must acknowledge before the write succeeds — you can lose 1 broker and still have a quorum. RF=5/min=5 is overkill and reduces availability.

questions.prompt: Kafka retention is set to 7 days. A consumer is down for 8 days. What happens?

options.text: Kafka holds the messages until the consumer catches up
Messages older than 7 days are deleted — consumer misses them permanently
Kafka emails an alert
The consumer group is automatically reset to the latest offset

questions.explanation: Kafka retention is time-based (or size-based), not consumer-driven. Old segments are deleted regardless of whether consumers have read them. Plan for long outages with longer retention or archiving to S3 via Kafka Connect.

questions.prompt: You need to ingest 100k events/sec from IoT devices. Design the Kafka topic structure, partitioning strategy, and consumer fleet. Justify partition count.

rubric.criterion: Partition count = max(throughput_needed / throughput_per_partition, consumer_parallelism). E.g. 100k events × 1KB = 100MB/s; single partition ~30MB/s write → 4 partitions min; use 64 for future scale.
Key by device_id for ordering per device
RF=3, min.insync=2, acks=all for durability
Consumer group per downstream job (analytics, alerting, storage)
Monitor consumer lag per partition; auto-scale consumer fleet on lag
Retention sized for replay window (7d default, or 30d + S3 offload)

questions.modelAnswer: Topic: iot-events, 64 partitions (100MB/s ÷ 30MB/s per partition ≈ 4 min, 64 for headroom + easy rebalance). Key = device_id → consistent partition → ordered processing per device. RF=3 (3 AZs), min.insync.replicas=2, producer acks=all. 3 consumer groups: (1) real-time analytics (Flink/ksqlDB), (2) alerting (threshold checks, low latency), (3) cold storage (Kafka Connect → S3 Parquet). Consumer fleet: auto-scale on lag metric (CloudWatch Kafka Consumer Lag → step scaling). Retention: 7d + compacted topic for latest-state-per-device. Brokers: 6 × i3.xlarge (NVMe) RF=3 across 3 AZs.

questions.prompt: Which are TRUE about Kafka ordering guarantees? (select all)

options.text: Messages are ordered globally across all partitions
Messages are ordered within a partition
Same key always maps to same partition (with fixed partition count)
You can achieve per-entity ordering by keying on entity ID
Kafka guarantees ordering across consumer group restarts

questions.explanation: Ordering is per-partition only. Same key → same partition (Murmur2 hash, fixed partition count). Per-entity ordering via entity key is the standard pattern. Global ordering is impossible with partitioned systems. Restarts preserve ordering within a partition (consumers re-read from committed offset).

questions.prompt: When do you use Kafka log compaction instead of time-based retention?

options.text: When you want to keep the LATEST value per key (changelog / event sourcing state)
When you want to compress old messages
When you want to replicate topics across clusters
When throughput is too high for time-based retention

questions.explanation: Log compaction retains only the latest record per key — useful for change-data-capture (CDC), materialised views, and config topics where you need the current state without full history.

questions.prompt: Which RabbitMQ exchange type should you use to broadcast a message to ALL bound queues?

options.text: direct
topic
fanout
headers

questions.explanation: Fanout exchange broadcasts to all bound queues regardless of routing key. direct = exact key match. topic = wildcard routing key patterns (#, *). headers = route by header attributes.

questions.prompt: A Lambda consuming SQS messages takes 35 seconds to process. The visibility timeout is 30s. What happens?

options.text: The message is deleted after 30s — processed or not
The message reappears in the queue at 30s and another consumer picks it up — duplicate processing
SQS waits for the Lambda to finish regardless of timeout
The message is sent to the DLQ

questions.explanation: Visibility timeout hides the message from other consumers during processing. If not deleted before the timeout expires, SQS makes it visible again → duplicate processing. Fix: set visibility timeout ≥ max processing time, or use ChangeMessageVisibility to extend it mid-processing.

questions.prompt: When should you choose SQS FIFO over SQS Standard?

options.text: Always — FIFO is strictly better
When message ordering AND exactly-once processing are required (e.g. financial transactions)
When you need > 300 TPS
FIFO is cheaper

questions.explanation: FIFO guarantees ordering per MessageGroupId and exactly-once within a 5-minute dedup window. Tradeoff: 300 TPS limit (3,000 with batching) vs Standard's nearly unlimited. Use FIFO for ordered workflows (e-commerce state machines, payments). Use Standard for high-throughput fan-out.

questions.prompt: A message in an SQS queue has been received 5 times and never deleted. What should happen?

options.text: SQS deletes it automatically after 5 receives
It stays in the queue indefinitely
SQS moves it to the configured Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) after maxReceiveCount is exceeded
SQS doubles its visibility timeout

questions.explanation: Configure a DLQ on the source queue with maxReceiveCount (e.g. 5). After 5 failed receive-delete cycles, SQS automatically moves the message to the DLQ for inspection, replay, or alerting. Always configure a DLQ in production.

questions.prompt: Why should you use SQS long polling (WaitTimeSeconds=20) instead of short polling?

options.text: Long polling is required for FIFO queues
Reduces empty API responses, lowers cost, and decreases latency when messages arrive
Short polling can miss messages
Long polling is faster because it uses WebSockets

questions.explanation: Short polling samples a subset of SQS servers and may return empty even when messages exist. Long polling waits up to 20s for a message — eliminates empty responses, reduces ReceiveMessage API cost, and delivers messages faster on arrival.

questions.prompt: Design a reliable order processing pipeline using SQS. Orders must be processed exactly once, in order per customer, with automatic retry and alerting on poison-pill orders.

rubric.criterion: SQS FIFO with MessageGroupId = customer_id for per-customer ordering
Idempotency key (order_id) as deduplication ID — FIFO's 5-min exactly-once window
Visibility timeout ≥ max processing time; extend with ChangeMessageVisibility if needed
Dead Letter Queue with maxReceiveCount=5; CloudWatch alarm on DLQ depth
Consumer deletes message AFTER successful downstream write (not before)
DLQ replay mechanism + human review for poison pills

questions.modelAnswer: SQS FIFO queue: MessageGroupId = customer_id (per-customer order), MessageDeduplicationId = order_id (exactly-once, 5-min window). Consumer: Lambda or ECS task. Flow: receive message → idempotency check (DynamoDB SET IF NOT EXISTS on order_id) → process → write result → delete message. Visibility timeout = 120s (set higher than P99 processing time). ChangeMessageVisibility heartbeat if processing can exceed that. DLQ on main queue: maxReceiveCount=5. CloudWatch: alarm if DLQ ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible > 0. Ops runbook: inspect DLQ, fix bug, replay via SQS console or script.

questions.prompt: Which are valid reasons to choose RabbitMQ over Kafka? (select all)

options.text: Complex per-message routing (topic exchanges, header-based routing)
Need to replay events days later from a consumer that was offline
Traditional task queues where messages are consumed and deleted
Sub-millisecond latency for small message volumes
Ingesting millions of events per second for analytics

questions.explanation: RabbitMQ: better for complex routing, task queues (message deleted on ack), and low-latency small-scale. Kafka: better for high-throughput event streaming, long-term retention, and replay. Kafka's retention makes offline-consumer replay easy; RabbitMQ discards acked messages.

questions.prompt: In a Node.js Writable stream, write() returns false. What should the caller do?

options.text: Retry immediately — false just means try again
Stop writing and wait for the 'drain' event before resuming
Close the stream — false means it failed
Switch to synchronous write mode

questions.explanation: write() returning false means the internal buffer is full — the stream is applying backpressure. The caller must stop writing and listen for the 'drain' event, which fires when the buffer is below the highWaterMark. Ignoring this causes unbounded memory growth.

questions.prompt: Why should you prefer readable.pipe(writable) over manually calling write() in a loop?

options.text: pipe() is synchronous and faster
pipe() automatically handles backpressure — it pauses the readable when the writable buffer is full
Manual write() doesn't support binary data
pipe() compresses data automatically

questions.explanation: pipe() wires up the drain and pause signals automatically. The readable is paused when write() returns false and resumed on drain. Manual loops that ignore the return value of write() will overwhelm the writable and consume unbounded memory.

questions.prompt: Your service writes to a downstream queue. The queue depth is growing unboundedly. What's the right backpressure strategy?

options.text: Increase queue size limit
Add more producers to catch up
Apply backpressure to producers: pause intake, scale consumers, or shed load via rate limiting
Drop all new messages until queue clears

questions.explanation: Unbounded queue depth = consumers can't keep up. Correct responses: (1) propagate backpressure upstream to pause producers, (2) scale consumers, (3) shed load with a leaky bucket if the system is overloaded. Dropping silently is lossy; just growing the queue defers the problem.

questions.prompt: Token bucket vs leaky bucket rate limiting: which allows bursting?

options.text: Leaky bucket — it smooths output regardless of input burst
Token bucket — accumulated tokens allow short bursts above the average rate
Both allow the same burst behavior
Neither — both enforce strict rates

questions.explanation: Token bucket accumulates tokens at a steady rate (up to bucket max). A burst can consume all stored tokens at once → allows short bursts. Leaky bucket drains at a fixed rate regardless of input → strict smoothing, no bursting.

questions.prompt: Design end-to-end backpressure for a pipeline: HTTP ingest → Kafka → stream processor → PostgreSQL. What happens at each stage when Postgres is slow?

rubric.criterion: Postgres slow → stream processor write latency rises → processor pauses consuming Kafka partitions
Kafka consumer lag rises → alert fires → auto-scale processors
If lag still rising: HTTP ingest returns 503/429 (load shedding at edge)
Kafka's durable retention acts as a buffer — no data loss during the slowdown
Postgres connection pool saturation → circuit breaker or bulkhead to limit damage
Monitoring: Postgres latency → consumer lag → ingest 5xx rate as cascade alert chain

questions.modelAnswer: Postgres slow → writer latency spikes → processor's in-flight batch doesn't complete → consumer pauses Kafka partition reads (Kafka backpressure: pause(partitions) API). Consumer lag builds. Alert: consumer lag > 50k events fires auto-scale (add processor pods). If Postgres is truly degraded (circuit breaker open), processor drops to minimal throughput. Kafka holds messages safely for the retention window. At ingest: if lag > threshold for 60s, API gateway returns 429 with Retry-After header to shed load at source. Recovery: Postgres heals → circuit breaker half-opens → processor resumes partitions → lag drains → 429s stop. Monitoring: multi-tier alert — Postgres p99 > 500ms → consumer lag > 10k → ingest 429 rate > 5% (each tier is both a symptom and a trigger).

questions.prompt: When should you prefer optimistic locking over pessimistic locking in a database?

options.text: When conflicts are frequent and you want to avoid retries
When conflicts are rare — it avoids lock overhead in the happy path
Optimistic locking is always faster
When rows are locked for long-running operations

questions.explanation: Optimistic: read row, check version on write; retry on conflict. No lock held during think time → high throughput when conflicts are rare. Pessimistic: hold lock for entire operation → safe when conflicts are frequent or consistency is critical (e.g. inventory deduction).

questions.prompt: What is a Saga pattern and why use it instead of a distributed 2PC transaction?

options.text: Saga is a database technique for row-level locking across shards
Saga sequences local transactions with compensating actions on failure — avoids distributed locks and the availability/latency cost of 2PC
Saga is an event sourcing pattern
Saga and 2PC are equivalent; saga is just newer

questions.explanation: 2PC requires all participants to lock resources until the coordinator commits/aborts — slow, availability risk if coordinator fails. Saga: each service commits its local transaction and publishes an event. On failure a compensating transaction rolls back completed steps. Choreography (events) or orchestration (saga orchestrator). Tradeoff: eventual consistency vs 2PC's strong consistency.

questions.prompt: What are the three states of a circuit breaker and what triggers each transition?

options.text: Open → Closed → Half-open; triggers: timeout, recovery, retry
Closed → Open → Half-open; triggers: error threshold, timer, probe success
Healthy → Degraded → Failed; triggers: latency, error rate, timeout
Idle → Active → Tripped; triggers: load, errors, reset

questions.explanation: Closed (normal) → Open (error rate exceeds threshold, e.g. >50% in 30s) → Half-open (after cooldown timer, send probe requests) → Closed (probe succeeds) or back to Open (probe fails). Prevents cascading failures by fast-failing requests when downstream is unhealthy.

questions.prompt: What problem does the Bulkhead pattern solve?

options.text: Rate limiting external API calls
Isolating resource pools so one slow dependency can't exhaust all threads/connections and take down unrelated services
Load balancing across replicas
Encrypting inter-service communication

questions.explanation: Named after ship bulkheads that isolate compartments. If Service A and Service B share one connection pool and B becomes slow, A's requests also pile up and exhaust the pool. Bulkhead: separate pools per dependency so slow B only affects B's pool.

questions.prompt: You need to update a database row AND publish a Kafka event atomically. What pattern ensures no event is lost even if the app crashes after the DB write?

options.text: 2-phase commit between Postgres and Kafka
Outbox pattern: write event to an outbox table in the same DB transaction, then poll/CDC to publish to Kafka
Publish to Kafka first, then write to DB
Write to both in a try/catch

questions.explanation: Outbox pattern: event row goes into the outbox table inside the same local DB transaction as the business data write. A separate relay (polling or CDC via Debezium) reads the outbox and publishes to Kafka, then marks events as sent. Crash between DB write and Kafka publish → relay retries → at-least-once delivery guaranteed.

questions.prompt: A payment API is called twice with the same idempotency key due to a network retry. What should happen?

options.text: Process both — more transactions are fine
Return the same response as the first call without processing the payment again
Return 409 Conflict
Return 400 Bad Request

questions.explanation: The server stores (idempotency_key, response) in a durable store. On duplicate request: return the cached response immediately. The client retries safely without double-charging. Standard pattern for Stripe, AWS SDK, etc.

questions.prompt: Design a distributed rate limiter for an API: 1000 req/min per user across N app servers. Needs to work correctly even when requests hit different servers.

rubric.criterion: Centralized counter in Redis — the only correct option for distributed enforcement
Token bucket or sliding window counter algorithm
Redis INCR + EXPIRE for fixed window; or sorted set for sliding window
Key: rate_limit:{user_id}:{window} — per-user, per-time-window
Atomic operations: INCR is atomic; use Lua script for check-then-set to avoid races
Return 429 with Retry-After header; expose X-RateLimit-Remaining header

questions.modelAnswer: Redis-backed sliding window counter. Key: ratelimit:{user_id}:{minute_bucket} (e.g. ratelimit:u123:202609011430). Lua script: INCR key; if result = 1, EXPIRE key 120 (two windows for safety). If count > 1000 → 429 Too Many Requests + Retry-After: {seconds_until_next_window} + X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0. For smoother sliding window: ZADD ratelimit:{user_id} timestamp timestamp; ZREMRANGEBYSCORE 0 now-60s; ZCARD — count in window. Redis single-threaded → ZADD+ZREMRANGE+ZCARD in a Lua script is atomic. Fallback if Redis is down: fail open (allow request) or fail closed (deny) — configure per product requirement. Local in-memory cache as L1 for common paths to reduce Redis calls.

questions.prompt: A cached value expires at midnight. 10,000 concurrent requests all get a cache miss simultaneously. What problem is this and how do you fix it?

options.text: Cache stampede / thundering herd. Fix: probabilistic early expiration or a mutex/promise-lock so only one request rebuilds the cache
Cache invalidation bug. Fix: use write-through caching
TTL too short. Fix: increase TTL
Database connection pool exhaustion. Fix: increase pool size

questions.explanation: Cache stampede: all requests see stale/missing cache and slam the database simultaneously. Fixes: (1) mutex — first miss acquires lock, others wait for rebuilt value; (2) XFetch probabilistic early expiration — recompute before expiry with a probability that rises as TTL decreases; (3) stale-while-revalidate — serve stale while rebuilding in background.

questions.prompt: What problem does CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) solve?

options.text: Encrypting commands separately from queries
Separating read and write models so each can be optimised independently — writes go to normalised DB, reads from denormalised read store
Preventing concurrent writes to the same row
Batching queries to reduce DB connections

questions.explanation: CQRS: commands (writes) update the authoritative write model; events propagate to a separate read model (Elasticsearch, Redis, materialised views) optimised for queries. Tradeoff: eventual consistency between write and read stores, more infrastructure complexity.

questions.prompt: Which are REAL risks with distributed locks (e.g. Redis SET NX EX)? (select all)

options.text: Lock holder crashes before releasing — lock expires after TTL, but work was incomplete
Clock drift causes premature expiry — holder still running but lock released
Redis leader failover — replica may not have the lock key yet (Redlock exists to mitigate)
Two processes acquire the lock simultaneously on a single-node Redis
Long GC pause causes holder to believe it still holds the lock after TTL expiry

questions.explanation: D is wrong — single-node Redis SET NX is atomic, so two processes can't both succeed. All others are real: crash before release (TTL saves you but leaves work partial), clock drift (NTP sync helps), Redis failover (Redlock uses N masters), and GC pause causing 'fencing token' violations (use fencing tokens for strong safety).

questions.prompt: When should you use Kafka Connect instead of writing a custom Kafka consumer?

options.text: Always — Kafka Connect is always better
For standard source/sink integrations (Postgres CDC, S3, Elasticsearch) where a connector exists — avoids boilerplate offset management and fault tolerance
Only for S3 sinks
When throughput is too high for custom consumers

questions.explanation: Kafka Connect provides a framework for connectors with built-in offset storage, fault tolerance, scalability, and a REST management API. For commodity integrations (JDBC source, Debezium CDC, S3 sink, Elasticsearch sink) it's the right choice. Write a custom consumer when business logic is non-trivial or no connector exists.

questions.prompt: A Kafka consumer group rebalances mid-processing. What's the safest offset commit strategy to avoid data loss?

options.text: Auto-commit with enable.auto.commit=true
Commit offset AFTER successful downstream write, using manual synchronous commit
Commit offset BEFORE processing to avoid reprocessing on restart
Use async commit for all offsets

questions.explanation: Auto-commit can commit before processing completes → data loss on crash. Commit-before-processing = skip messages. Correct: commit AFTER the downstream is durably written. Synchronous commit on rebalance (use onPartitionsRevoked callback) to flush in-flight work. Async commit is fine mid-batch but sync on shutdown/rebalance.

questions.prompt: SQS Lambda trigger is processing messages one at a time. How do you increase throughput?

options.text: Increase Lambda memory — more memory = more SQS throughput
Set BatchSize (up to 10k for Standard, 10 for FIFO) and increase concurrency — Lambda processes multiple messages per invocation
Switch to SQS FIFO — it has higher throughput
Set WaitTimeSeconds=0 for faster polling

questions.explanation: SQS event source mapping for Lambda: BatchSize controls messages per invocation (up to 10,000 for Standard queues). Reserved concurrency or auto-scaling controls parallel Lambda instances. FIFO is capped at 300/3k TPS — lower than Standard, not higher.

questions.prompt: Two worker threads read and write the same SharedArrayBuffer counter without synchronization. What happens?

options.text: They take turns automatically — SharedArrayBuffer is thread-safe
Race condition — reads and writes can interleave, producing incorrect results
The second thread blocks until the first is done
Node.js throws a RangeError

questions.explanation: SharedArrayBuffer allows true shared memory between threads — but it's not synchronized. Use Atomics.add(), Atomics.compareExchange(), or a mutex pattern (Atomics.wait/Atomics.notify) to safely coordinate concurrent access.

questions.prompt: Design a background job queue for a SaaS: users trigger async jobs (report generation, emails, exports). Jobs can take 1s–10min. Support prioritisation, retries, and progress updates to the UI.

rubric.criterion: Persistent queue (Bull/BullMQ on Redis, or SQS, or Postgres-backed) — not in-memory
Priority queues: high (emails/alerts), normal (exports), low (reports)
Retry with exponential backoff + max retry count + DLQ
Job state stored durably: pending → active → completed | failed | retrying
Progress updates via WebSocket or SSE polling job status endpoint
Worker auto-scaling based on queue depth; concurrency limit per worker
Timeout: kill hung jobs after max duration, mark as failed

questions.modelAnswer: Use BullMQ (Redis-backed) with 3 named queues: high-priority, normal, low. Job payload stored in Redis; job state machine: waiting → active → completed | failed. Each worker pulls from highest-priority non-empty queue first. Retry: exponential backoff (1s, 4s, 16s, 64s), maxAttempts=5, then DLQ queue. Progress: worker calls job.updateProgress(pct) → stored in Redis → UI polls GET /api/jobs/:id or subscribes via SSE. Worker timeout: job.opts.jobTimeout=600000 (10 min); BullMQ kills timed-out jobs and marks failed. Auto-scaling: CloudWatch / custom metric on queue depth → ECS service scaling policy. UI: job list page shows status + progress bar; toast on completion via WebSocket subscription.

questions.prompt: Your Kafka consumer's downstream (a database) is slow. How do you apply backpressure properly without losing messages?

options.text: Drop messages when the database is slow
Call consumer.pause(partitions) when the downstream is overloaded, and consumer.resume(partitions) when it recovers — messages stay safely in Kafka
Increase fetch.max.bytes to buffer more messages locally
Lower the consumer's max.poll.interval.ms

questions.explanation: Kafka's consumer.pause()/consumer.resume() API stops fetching from specified partitions without losing messages (they stay in Kafka until consumer lag is caught up). This is the correct backpressure signal in a Kafka consumer. Lowering max.poll.interval.ms would cause rebalances.

questions.prompt: How does Kafka achieve exactly-once semantics end-to-end in a stream processing pipeline?

options.text: Enable enable.idempotence=true on the producer — that's all
Use Kafka Transactions: producer transactional.id + begin/commit transaction wrapping consume-process-produce, with isolation.level=read_committed on consumers
Exactly-once is impossible in distributed systems
Use Kafka Streams only — other clients can't achieve EOS

questions.explanation: Idempotent producer (enable.idempotence) prevents duplicate producer writes. For consume-transform-produce EOS: wrap in a transaction (beginTransaction → produce output → sendOffsetsToTransaction → commitTransaction). Downstream consumers with isolation.level=read_committed see only committed records.

questions.prompt: Why does fs.readFile not block the Node.js event loop even though disk I/O is synchronous at the OS level?

options.text: Node.js uses async kernel syscalls for all I/O
libuv offloads blocking I/O to a thread pool (default 4 threads); the event loop gets a callback when done
Node.js uses memory-mapped files to avoid disk reads
The OS handles async I/O transparently

questions.explanation: libuv maintains a thread pool (UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE, default 4). Blocking calls like filesystem I/O, DNS resolution, and crypto run on pool threads. When complete, a callback is queued on the event loop. The JS thread is never blocked. Increase UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE for I/O-heavy workloads.

questions.prompt: Which are genuine benefits of event sourcing? (select all)

options.text: Complete audit trail — every state change is recorded
Time travel — replay events to rebuild state at any point in time
Simpler queries — read from the event log directly
Natural integration with event-driven systems — events feed downstream consumers
Eliminates need for a relational database

questions.explanation: Event sourcing: A (full audit log), B (replay to any past state), D (events naturally feed Kafka/queue consumers). C is wrong — querying the event log is complex; you need read models (CQRS) for efficient queries. E is wrong — you still need a projection store for current state queries.

questions.prompt: PostgreSQL uses MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control). Why does a SELECT not block concurrent INSERTs/UPDATEs?

options.text: PostgreSQL holds no locks for SELECT — it reads at any time
Each transaction sees a snapshot of the database at its start; writes create new row versions rather than overwriting — readers and writers don't block each other
PostgreSQL uses a global read lock that allows concurrent reads
SELECT is non-transactional in PostgreSQL

questions.explanation: MVCC: each write creates a new version of a row with transaction ID metadata (xmin/xmax). Readers see the snapshot consistent with their transaction's start. No shared read locks → high read concurrency. Vacuum reclaims old versions (dead tuples). This is why REPEATABLE READ isolation is cheap in Postgres.
